Lewin's honeyeater (Meliphaga lewinii) is a common resident of rainforest canopies along Australia's eastern coast, and its life-history strategy reflects the relatively stable, productive environments it occupies. Neonates emerge from eggs incubated at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days], a hatching interval that is typical for honeyeaters of its body size. The very small initial wet weight of newly hatched chicks, recorded at a mere 4.22 grams [Ww0 = 4.22 grams], is consistent with an altricial mode of development in which the nestling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrition. This modest mass at hatching marks the beginning of a rapid growth trajectory that carries the chick through a well-defined sequence of developmental milestones over the subsequent weeks of nest life. Field observations indicate that the nestling phase proceeds steadily under the relatively warm thermal conditions typical of subtropical lowland forests, where ambient temperatures during the breeding season frequently approach the species' active metabolic range.

Growth proceeds rapidly during the nestling stage, and one of the earliest key transitions is the achievement of fledging. The time since birth at fledging has been documented at 15 days since birth [tx = 15 days since birth] under the thermal conditions typical of lowland breeding sites in summer, when daytime temperatures often reach 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of many Australian honeyeaters and reflects a trade-off between the demands of predator avoidance and the energetic costs of extended brooding in a warm climate. After leaving the nest, the fledgling continues to be fed by both parents for several additional weeks while its flight muscles and foraging skills develop. Somatic growth does not cease upon fledging, however, and the bird continues to gain mass steadily through the juvenile and sub-adult stages. Ultimately, the ultimate wet weight for males reaches an average of 40.2 grams [Wwi = 40.2 grams], while females, which are slightly smaller on average, attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 33.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 33.9 grams], with broader ranges of 27.5 to 49.5 grams for males and 27.3 to 41.5 grams for females recorded across various populations.

Puberty, defined here as the achievement of full gonadal maturation and the capacity to breed, is not reached immediately after fledging. The time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 45 days since birth [tp = 45 days since birth] under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active metabolic period (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), a relatively short developmental delay that suggests a fast life-history pace for a bird of this body mass. Indeed, the onset of reproductive competence at approximately six weeks of age is notably early compared to many other passerines of equivalent size, which often delay maturity for several months. This accelerated maturation is likely linked to the high productivity of rainforest habitats, where abundant fruit and invertebrate prey allow young birds to accumulate the necessary somatic reserves quickly. Following the attainment of puberty, individuals do not immediately commence breeding, as they typically require a period of territory establishment and social integration before their first reproductive attempt. The interval between hatching and first successful breeding is thus a key demographic parameter.

First reproduction is typically deferred until the individual has had time to secure a territory and form a stable pair bond, both of which are necessary for successful nesting in this resident, socially monogamous species. The time since birth at first brood has been measured at 1.3 years since birth [tR = 1.3 years since birth] under the thermal conditions of the species' active metabolic range (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), a delay that reflects the challenges of territory acquisition in saturated lowland forests. Once a bird has established itself, the species is capable of sustained reproductive effort. Under the same warm thermal conditions, the maximum reproduction rate is achieved: females can produce approximately three broods per year [F_R_i = approximately three broods per year], with each brood typically consisting of a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], yielding an overall annual output of roughly three nesting attempts per year. This high reproductive frequency is made possible by the extended breeding season in subtropical regions.

The physiological machinery that supports this rapid pace of life includes a relatively elevated metabolic rate. Basal metabolic rate, measured as resting oxygen consumption under standard conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reaches 96 milliliters per hour [JOi = 96 milliliters per hour], a value that is consistent with the high metabolic demands of a small, active nectivore-omnivore inhabiting warm climates. This elevated metabolic expenditure, coupled with the energetic demands of frequent breeding, likely imposes physiological costs that limit maximum longevity. Indeed, despite the fast pace of development and reproduction, the maximum lifespan of Lewin's honeyeater is moderate: the oldest documented individual reached an age of 12.5 years since birth [am = 12.5 years since birth] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan of roughly twelve and a half years is comparable to that of other medium-sized Australian honeyeaters and suggests a life-history strategy that balances high reproductive output against a relatively extended period of adult survival.
